paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 5.18 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 5 (Part 8)
paragraphs.text: (1) Subject to subrules (2) and (3), if (a) a party cannot obtain relevant and material information from an officer or employee or a former officer or former employee of a corporation or partnership that is a party adverse in interest, (b) it would be unfair to require the party seeking the information to proceed to trial without having the opportunity to ask questions about the information sought, and (c) the questioning will not cause undue hardship, expense or delay to, or unfairness to, any other party or to the person to be questioned, the party may question, under oath, a person who has provided services for the corporation or partnership and who can provide the best evidence on the issue. (2) A person described in subrule (1) may be questioned only (a) by written agreement of the parties, or (b) with the Court's permission. (3) An expert engaged by a party for the purposes of the action may not be questioned under this rule. (4) Evidence from a person questioned under this rule is to be treated as if it were evidence of an employee of the corporation or partnership. (5) The costs related to questioning a person under this rule are to be borne by the questioning party unless (a) the parties otherwise agree, or (b) the Court otherwise orders. Alta. Reg. 36/2020, s. 7

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.18:1 Rule 5.18 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.18. In 1218388 Alberta Ltd. v. Reifel Cooke Group Limited, 2019 ABQB 76, 2019 CarswellAlta 206, Madam Justice Grosse gave this overview of R. 5.18: [36] Rule 5.18 is not a third party discovery rule. In Alberta, we do not have pre-trial discovery of mere witnesses. Parties are generally limited to questioning other parties prior to trial. Rules like 5.17(1)(b) and 5.18 are in place in recognition of the fact that a corporation only acts and speaks through people, and often, relevant and material information of a corporation will be spread across multiple people. Rule 5.18 applies only to corporate parties. [37] In the pre-2010 Rules of Court, Rule 200 was the applicable rule. It referred only to employees and officers of corporate parties. Much jurisprudence developed as to who could be considered an employee or an officer and ultimately, the law recognized that people who carried out functions akin to an employee could be discovered even if they were an independent contractor, a consultant, a volunteer or some other role, other than a legal employee or officer. [38] In the Alberta Law Reform Institute Consultation Memorandum No. 12.2, “Document Discovery and Examination for Discovery”, the Committee recommended codifying this law by referring to service providers instead of to employees and officers. However, they rejected expanding discovery to include mere witnesses. The Court of Appeal has reiterated the point: Hunka v Waiward Steele Fabricators Ltd, 2011 ABCA 142 (CanLII) at para 21. [39] It is noteworthy that subparagraph (4) of Rule 5.18 allows the evidence obtained under this Rule to be put to the corporate representative, just like evidence of an employee. This is not a feature of all similar rules in other Canadian jurisdictions. In my view, it is significant when interpreting and applying the Alberta rule. Presumably, when determining whether Rules 5.18(1)(b) and (c) are satisfied in any particular case, among the relevant considerations are the nature of the information sought and the nature of the relationship between the corporate party litigant and the service provider vis à vis that information. In my view, the fact that a party relies on a consultant for advice in a particular area—even heavily—does not necessarily mean that the test will be satisfied. How the law would apply to the relationship between Shelby and RCGL in this case should be determined if further issues arise. In Cogent Group Inc. v. EnCana Leasehold Ltd. Partnership, 2011 ABQB 335, 2011 CarswellAlta 878, 520 A.R. 8 (Master), the Plaintiff wished to question a Mr. Crockford who had in the past been a service provider to EnCana Leasehold. Master Mason outlined the facts in paragraph 9: … While Mr. Crockford has provided some services to EnCana Leasehold in the past, it has not provided services to EnCana Leasehold in regard to the issues in this litigation. Cogent concedes that the knowledge sought to be elicited through questioning Mr. Crockford is unrelated to the past services he provided to EnCana Leasehold. The Plaintiff submitted that “the wording of Rule 5.18 does not require that the knowledge be acquired by virtue of the services provided to the party corporation.” The Plaintiff submitted that it had the right to question Crockford if the Plaintiff could show that Crockford had knowledge relevant to the current litigation and that he had been a service provider to EnCana Leasehold at some point. Master Mason disagreed. At paragraphs 24–30, the learned Master said: 24 Rule 5.18 does not expressly state that the information of the person sought to be questioned needs to have been acquired by virtue of the services provided to the corporate party. In my view, however, the purpose of the Rule is to allow questioning of persons akin to employees who have gained relevant and material knowledge as a result of providing services to a party corporation. The required connection is implicit in the rule and fundamental to the Alberta approach to questioning non-parties prior to trial. 25 At the hearing, I queried why an officer or employee could only be examined under Rule 5.17 if their relevant and material knowledge was obtained because of their employment or role as officer, yet a service provider would not similarly be subject to that requirement. Counsel for Cogent was not able to supply a rationale. 26 In my view, it would be inconsistent with the requirements of Rule 5.17 and former Rule 200, the judicial interpretation of which is now captured in Rule 5.18, to conclude that service providers who may have acquired relevant and material knowledge outside of the service relationship, can be questioned prior to trial in the same fashion as an employee of a party. It is the provision of services in relation to the matters at issue in the action that transforms a mere witness into a service provider within the meaning of Rule 5.18. 27 While I appreciate Mr. Crockford's role in the termination of the EnCana Power agreement, and that he appears to have relevant knowledge in this regard, there is no dispute that he gained this knowledge outside of his past role as a service provider to EnCana Leasehold. Those past services do not relate to the issues in this action. To borrow the words of Graesser J. in Harcap Investments Inc. v. Alberta Permit Pro Inc. at paragraph 23, just because Mr. Crockford may have something to say, does not make him subject to questioning. 28 Cogent submits that it is the corporate relationship between EnCana Leasehold and EnCana Power that most strongly supports its entitlement to question Mr. Crockford as a service provider of EnCana Leasehold. 29 It is important in this context to emphasize that Rule 5.18 requires the person sought to be questioned to have provided services to the party, and it is on the basis of the provision of services, not a corporate relationship or affiliation, that a person may be questioned under the rule. Relying on the corporate relationship between EnCana Leasehold and EnCana Power in order to access a rule based on the provision of services is not appropriate in my view. It is inconsistent with the genesis and purpose of Rule 5.18 and with basic principles of corporate law. 30 Mr. Crockford is not a service provider to EnCana Leasehold within the meaning of Rule 5.18. In CNOOC Petroleum North America ULC v. 801 Seventh Inc., 2023 ABCA 97, 2023 CarswellAlta 674, the Court said: “This rule was not intended to reverse the long-standing Alberta position that there is no pretrial questioning of non-party witnesses.” (paragraph 33). At paragraph 39, the Court said: “Rule 5.18 is not intended to displace the normal method of record production or questioning. The test in R. 5.18(1)(a) sets a high bar: ‘a party cannot obtain relevant and material information’ from the corporate representative. While the rule should not be read dogmatically, it cannot be invoked simply because it would be more convenient, or perhaps more efficient, to directly examine agents and consultants rather than having the information ‘funneled’ through the corporate representative….” (emphasis in original). At paragraph 50 of CNOOC Petroleum North America ULC v. 801 Seventh Inc., the Court said: “… Rule 5.18 is not a method to obtain expert opinions from consultants hired by an adverse party to assess risk, mitigate damages, or otherwise assist in the litigation.” 1. Application of R. 5.18 to entities which are also parties to the action In Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v. ShawCor Ltd., 2016 ABQB 21, Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. (CNRL) sued certain defendants alleging that the defendants had “negligently provided a pipe coating and insulation system related to a 32 kilometre underground pipeline owned by CNRL”. One of the defendants (ShawCor) issued a third party claim against Dunn Hiebert & Associates Ltd. (Dunn Hiebert). It was alleged that Dunn Hiebert provided to CNRL pipeline inspection services and had approved the coating provided by ShawCor. Another defendant (IMV) sought an order under R. 5.18(4) to treat its questioning of Tom Dunn (owner of Dunn Hiebert), Bill Smith (Assistant Chief Inspector for Dunn Hiebert), and Sursad Jamil (Dunn Hiebert inspector) as if it was questioning of employees of CNRL. Chief Justice Wittmann allowed the application. His Lordship said: 20 As stated, IMV and Flint have complied with ARC 5.18(1)(a) in that relevant and material evidence of construction management and inspection services on the pipeline project cannot be obtained from an officer or employee or former officer or former employee of CNRL. … 22 The Dunn Hiebert witnesses have been produced by Dunn Hiebert because Dunn Hiebert is a party to the action and questioning has been conducted by any party that has declared themselves adverse in interest to Dunn Hiebert. As put by CNRL, all of the “information sought by IMV and Flint has been obtained through the questioning of the Dunn Hiebert witnesses”. Thus, it is not unfair to IMV or Flint to require them to proceed to trial without the information because they have the information. 23 However, according to IMV and Flint, the unfairness arises because they cannot treat the evidence of the Dunn Hiebert witnesses as if it were given by employees of CNRL without the relief asked for. If granted, IMV and Flint will meet the threshold for the application of ARC 5.29 and 5.31. The purpose of questioning, formerly known as oral discovery, is not only to obtain information from an opposite party or a party adverse in interest, but also to obtain admissions against the interest of that opposite party or party adverse in interest that can be read-in at the trial. Flint and IMV say it is unfair for them not to be able to do this, if they find it necessary. 24 The Court is well aware of the practice that rarely do defendants find it necessary to read-in excerpts from the questioning of a plaintiff at trial. CNRL argued this. The dominant use of the questioning at trial by a defendant, whose case is usually not started until the plaintiff's case is in, is to confront witnesses who have been questioned under oath or affirmation, with a previous inconsistent statement pursuant to the procedure mandated in the Alberta Evidence Act, RSA 2000, c A-18, s. 22. In other words, the transcript is used for the purpose of cross-examining the plaintiff's witnesses who have been subject to questioning by defence counsel. Notwithstanding this practicality, the Court cannot anticipate whether a defendant, IMV or Flint, may choose to read-in questioning evidence against the plaintiff, as part of that defendant's case against the plaintiff. It would be wrong to base any decision on the basis that the practice rarely occurs. 25 In short, the Court sees no unfairness to CNRL by allowing the application of ARC 5.18 to occur even where the persons providing the services or the entity providing the services, within the meaning of ARC 5.18, is a party to the action. 26 The Court acknowledges that in The Alberta Law Reform Institute's Consultation Memorandum 12.2, this situation was not contemplated. The Court agrees with CNRL that what was contemplated in the Consultation Memorandum is that it would apply to persons or entities not a party in an action. CNRL argues ARC 5.18 was intended to apply only to “a stranger to the action”. 27 In Petro Canada Products Inc, employees of Dresser US were involved in doing the work contracted by Dresser-Rand Canada Inc. and the Court ordered those persons to be examinable under the old ARC 200 as being “akin” to employees. Dresser US was the sister company of Dress-Rand Canada. Accepting this case is codified somewhat by ARC 5.18, it contemplated not a stranger, but a member of the family, but nevertheless a non-party. The stated purpose encompasses all situations where a service provider has the only available evidence, stranger or not. 28 With respect to ARC 5.18(c), there is no undue hardship, expense or delay to CNRL or to any other person with respect to the questioning of the Dunn Hiebert witnesses. That has already occurred. Again, the alleged unfairness by CNRL is the ability of Flint and IMV to treat the evidence of the Dunn Hiebert witnesses as if that were evidence of employees of CNRL. 29 During oral argument, the Court posed this question to counsel for CNRL: If Dunn Hiebert were not a party to the action, would there be any argument that ARC 5.18 would not apply? Counsel for CNRL conceded that perhaps no valid argument would exist, but stated “that's not what we have here.” The Court agrees. But does the fact that Dunn Hiebert is a party change anything? Not in the circumstances of this case. 30 If a read-in answer is attempted in any case before a trial judge, the party may object that the answer is incomplete: ARC 5.31(3). Moreover, by making the declaration that the evidence of the Dunn Hiebert witnesses is to be treated as if it were the evidence of employees of CNRL, the Court is not ruling on any aspect of ARC 5.29. The Court acknowledges that in the IMV brief, it is stated that CNRL has refused to acknowledge the evidence of the Dunn Hiebert witnesses as some of the evidence of CNRL's corporate witness. Conclusion 31 The Court grants the applications of IMV and Flint. The evidence of the Dunn Hiebert witnesses is evidence from persons questioned under ARC 5.18 and its to be treated as if it were evidence of employees of CNRL: ARC 5.18(4). 2. Consultants In Stankovic v. 849450 Alberta Ltd., 2016 ABQB 677, 2016 CarswellAlta 2375 (Master), “[t]he issue being considered [was] whether the defendant can question a lawyer carrying on the private practice of law as an ‘employee’ of the plaintiff under Rule 5.17(1(d)” (paragraph 1). Master Prowse said: 3 In these reasons I will use the term “consultant” to mean someone carrying on a profession as a private practitioner. Consultants typically have their own premises and provide services for many clients. Often the manner in which they provide services is regulated by a professional regulatory body. Mr. Daniels is a consultant as I use that term. … 12 Under Rule 5.18 it is no longer necessary to categorize a consultant as an “officer” or an “employee”. All that is necessary is to satisfy the public policy criteria, which I would summarize as follows: (a) a party cannot obtain relevant and material information from an examination of the adverse party under Rule 5.17, (b) it would be unfair to require the party seeking the examination of the service provider to proceed to trial without having the opportunity to ask the service provider about the information sought, presumably because it deals with a key issue in the litigation, and (c) the questioning of the service provider will not cause undue hardship, expense or delay to, or unfairness to, the adverse party or the service provider. Rule 5.18 is restricted to services provided to a corporation 13 My comments under this heading deal with the situation where a consultant provides services to a corporation. 14 The first step ought to be to determine whether the consultant was in fact an officer or employee of the adverse party. 15 In my view, the term “employee” should be interpreted utilizing the substantial case law developed in the areas of employment law and tax law which deal with whether someone is or is not an employee. In other words, the old case law under Rule 200 should not be used to broaden the concept of who is or is not an employee. 16 If someone is a consultant, as defined at the outset of these reasons, they would typically not be considered to be an employee under that law. 17 If the consultant is not an employee or officer of the adverse corporate party, then the consultant can nevertheless be examined under Rule 5.18 if the public policy criteria listed in Rule 5.18 can be satisfied. 18 It makes no sense to me to have an applicant apply to examine a consultant of an adverse corporate party under Rule 5.17, and to use the public policy criteria under case law developed under old Rule 200 to determine if that consultant is providing services “akin to” or “analogous to” an employee, when that consultant (who is clearly a service provider under Rule 5.18) can be examined under similar public policy criteria specifically listed in Rule 5.18. 19 The case law under old Rule 200 is voluminous and the decisions are sometimes contradictory. Where a clear rule has been enacted to codify the previously created public policy criteria, it is not helpful to refer to those previous cases. 20 Rule 5.17 is narrower than old Rule 200 which uses the word “employed” rather than Rule 5.17, which uses the word “employee”. It is common for a person to say that they “employed” a consultant architect to design a building for them. It would not be normal grammatical useage for that client to describe the architect as their “employee”. 21 Where an application is made to examine a consultant of an adverse corporate party, the definition of “employee” under Rule 5.17 should in my view be restricted to the normal usage of that term for the following reasons: (i) Rule 5.17 was enacted concurrently with Rule 5.18. The Rules should be interpreted together to make sense of them, (ii) the wording of Rule 5.17, which uses “employee” is narrower than the wording of old Rule 200, which used “employed”, (iii) it is more consistent with access to justice for litigants to use the clear concise express public policy criteria in Rule 5.18 to seek the examination of a consultant service provider than to refer to the voluminous case law under old Rule 200. Where the services are provided to an individual rather than a corporation 22 Rule 5.18 deals with examining a services provider to a corporation. It does not apply where a consultant provides services to a natural person. In that circumstance, the applicant will be driven to use Rule 5.17 in an attempt to categorize the service provider as an employee of or officer of the adverse party. 23 I am not sure why Rule 5.18 was not worded to apply to examining a service provider to a natural person such as Mr. Stankovic. 24 I am unable to envisage a public policy reason for Rule 5.18 not applying to consultants who provide services to a natural person. 25 Where does this leave us? Am I to apply the old case law under Rule 200 to see whether the definition of “employee” under Rule 5.17 can be “broadened” so as to encompass Mr. Daniels, just as the definitions of “employed” and “officer” were broadened by case law under the old Rule 200? 26 The public policy criteria discussed in the previous case law under Rule 200 has effectively been codified under Rule 5.18. Rather than litigants resorting back to that prior case law, with all the time and expense involved, I believe the criteria under Rule 5.18 should be applied to the application to examine Mr. Daniels under Rule 5.17, even though Mr. Daniel's services were provided to a natural person and not to a corporation. 27 In other words, in my view the definition of “employee” under Rule 5.17 should be broadened to cover Mr. Daniels only if: (a) the defendant 849 cannot obtain relevant and material information from an examination of Mr. Stankovic as a party adverse in interest, (b) it would be unfair to require the defendant 849 to proceed to trial without having the opportunity to ask Mr. Daniels about the information sought given the importance of that information, and (c) the questioning of Mr. Daniels will not cause undue hardship, expense or delay to, or unfairness to, the plaintiff Mr. Stankovic or to Mr. Daniels. … 47 For the reasons set out above, in my view, when an application is made to examine under oath a lawyer (or any other service provider) to an adverse party, the following process should be followed: (i) If the lawyer is or was an employee of the adverse party, then she/he may be examined for discovery under Rule 5.17. (ii) If the lawyer is not an employee of an adverse corporate party, but provided services to the adverse corporate party, then the application to compel the lawyers attendance at discovery should proceed under Rule 5.18. (iii) If the lawyer is not an employee, and the adverse party is an individual as opposed to a corporation, the court should have reference to the criteria listed under Rule 5.18 in deciding whether to allow discovery to take place, even though the application is not proceeding under Rule 5.18.

27 In Petro Canada Products Inc, employees of Dresser US were involved in doing the work contracted by Dresser-Rand Canada Inc. and the Court ordered those persons to be examinable under the old ARC 200 as being “akin” to employees.
Dresser US was the sister company of Dress-Rand Canada.
Accepting this case is codified somewhat by ARC 5.18, it contemplated not a stranger, but a member of the family, but nevertheless a non-party.
The stated purpose encompasses all situations where a service provider has the only available evidence, stranger or not.
28 With respect to ARC 5.18(c), there is no undue hardship, expense or delay to CNRL or to any other person with respect to the questioning of the Dunn Hiebert witnesses.
That has already occurred.
Again, the alleged unfairness by CNRL is the ability of Flint and IMV to treat the evidence of the Dunn Hiebert witnesses as if that were evidence of employees of CNRL.
29 During oral argument, the Court posed this question to counsel for CNRL: If Dunn Hiebert were not a party to the action, would there be any argument that ARC 5.18 would not apply?
Counsel for CNRL conceded that perhaps no valid argument would exist, but stated “that's not what we have here.” The Court agrees.
But does the fact that Dunn Hiebert is a party change anything?
Not in the circumstances of this case.
30 If a read-in answer is attempted in any case before a trial judge, the party may object that the answer is incomplete: ARC 5.31(3).

Moreover, by making the declaration that the evidence of the Dunn Hiebert witnesses is to be treated as if it were the evidence of employees of CNRL, the Court is not ruling on any aspect of ARC 5.29.
The Court acknowledges that in the IMV brief, it is stated that CNRL has refused to acknowledge the evidence of the Dunn Hiebert witnesses as some of the evidence of CNRL's corporate witness.
Conclusion 31 The Court grants the applications of IMV and Flint.
The evidence of the Dunn Hiebert witnesses is evidence from persons questioned under ARC 5.18 and its to be treated as if it were evidence of employees of CNRL: ARC 5.18(4).
Consultants In Stankovic v.

849450 Alberta Ltd., 2016 ABQB 677, 2016 CarswellAlta 2375 (Master), “[t]he issue being considered [was] whether the defendant can question a lawyer carrying on the private practice of law as an ‘employee’ of the plaintiff under Rule 5.17(1(d)” (paragraph 1).
Master Prowse said: 3 In these reasons I will use the term “consultant” to mean someone carrying on a profession as a private practitioner.
Consultants typically have their own premises and provide services for many clients.
Often the manner in which they provide services is regulated by a professional regulatory body.
Mr.
Daniels is a consultant as I use that term. … 12 Under Rule 5.18 it is no longer necessary to categorize a consultant as an “officer” or an “employee”.
All that is necessary is to satisfy the public policy criteria, which I would summarize as follows:
(a) a party cannot obtain relevant and material information from an examination of the adverse party under Rule 5.17

(b) it would be unfair to require the party seeking the examination of the service provider to proceed to trial without having the opportunity to ask the service provider about the information sought, presumably because it deals with a key issue in the litigation, and
(c) the questioning of the service provider will not cause undue hardship, expense or delay to, or unfairness to, the adverse party or the service provider.
Rule 5.18 is restricted to services provided to a corporation 13 My comments under this heading deal with the situation where a consultant provides services to a corporation.
14 The first step ought to be to determine whether the consultant was in fact an officer or employee of the adverse party.

15 In my view, the term “employee” should be interpreted utilizing the substantial case law developed in the areas of employment law and tax law which deal with whether someone is or is not an employee.
In other words, the old case law under Rule 200 should not be used to broaden the concept of who is or is not an employee.
16 If someone is a consultant, as defined at the outset of these reasons, they would typically not be considered to be an employee under that law.

17 If the consultant is not an employee or officer of the adverse corporate party, then the consultant can nevertheless be examined under Rule 5.18 if the public policy criteria listed in Rule 5.18 can be satisfied.

18 It makes no sense to me to have an applicant apply to examine a consultant of an adverse corporate party under Rule 5.17, and to use the public policy criteria under case law developed under old Rule 200 to determine if that consultant is providing services “akin to” or “analogous to” an employee, when that consultant (who is clearly a service provider under Rule 5.18) can be examined under similar public policy criteria specifically listed in Rule 5.18.
19 The case law under old Rule 200 is voluminous and the decisions are sometimes contradictory.
Where a clear rule has been enacted to codify the previously created public policy criteria, it is not helpful to refer to those previous cases.
20 Rule 5.17 is narrower than old Rule 200 which uses the word “employed” rather than Rule 5.17, which uses the word “employee”.
It is common for a person to say that they “employed” a consultant architect to design a building for them.
It would not be normal grammatical useage for that client to describe the architect as their “employee”.

21 Where an application is made to examine a consultant of an adverse corporate party, the definition of “employee” under Rule 5.17 should in my view be restricted to the normal usage of that term for the following reasons:
(i) Rule 5.17 was enacted concurrently with Rule 5.18.
The Rules should be interpreted together to make sense of them
(ii) the wording of Rule 5.17, which uses “employee” is narrower than the wording of old Rule 200, which used “employed”

(iii) it is more consistent with access to justice for litigants to use the clear concise express public policy criteria in Rule 5.18 to seek the examination of a consultant service provider than to refer to the voluminous case law under old Rule 200.
Where the services are provided to an individual rather than a corporation 22 Rule 5.18 deals with examining a services provider to a corporation.
It does not apply where a consultant provides services to a natural person.
In that circumstance, the applicant will be driven to use Rule 5.17 in an attempt to categorize the service provider as an employee of or officer of the adverse party.
23 I am not sure why Rule 5.18 was not worded to apply to examining a service provider to a natural person such as Mr.
Stankovic.
24 I am unable to envisage a public policy reason for Rule 5.18 not applying to consultants who provide services to a natural person.
25 Where does this leave us?
Am I to apply the old case law under Rule 200 to see whether the definition of “employee” under Rule 5.17 can be “broadened” so as to encompass Mr.
Daniels, just as the definitions of “employed” and “officer” were broadened by case law under the old Rule 200?
26 The public policy criteria discussed in the previous case law under Rule 200 has effectively been codified under Rule 5.18.
Rather than litigants resorting back to that prior case law, with all the time and expense involved, I believe the criteria under Rule 5.18 should be applied to the application to examine Mr.
Daniels under Rule 5.17, even though Mr.
Daniel's services were provided to a natural person and not to a corporation.
27 In other words, in my view the definition of “employee” under Rule 5.17 should be broadened to cover Mr.
Daniels only if: (a) the defendant 849 cannot obtain relevant and material information from an examination of Mr.
Stankovic as a party adverse in interest, (b) it would be unfair to require the defendant 849 to proceed to trial without having the opportunity to ask Mr.
Daniels about the information sought given the importance of that information, and (c) the questioning of Mr.
Daniels will not cause undue hardship, expense or delay to, or unfairness to, the plaintiff Mr.
Stankovic or to Mr.

Daniels. … 47 For the reasons set out above, in my view, when an application is made to examine under oath a lawyer (or any other service provider) to an adverse party, the following process should be followed:
(i) If the lawyer is or was an employee of the adverse party, then she/he may be examined for discovery under Rule 5.17.

(ii) If the lawyer is not an employee of an adverse corporate party, but provided services to the adverse corporate party, then the application to compel the lawyers attendance at discovery should proceed under Rule 5.18.

(iii) If the lawyer is not an employee, and the adverse party is an individual as opposed to a corporation, the court should have reference to the criteria listed under Rule 5.18 in deciding whether to allow discovery to take place, even though the application is not proceeding under Rule 5.18.

sentences.text: Limit or cancellation of questioning

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.19:1 Rule 5.19 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.19. In Pembina Pipeline Corporation v. Coney, 2019 ABQB 699, 2019 CarswellAlta 1962, Justice Romaine had before her an application to limit the number of witnesses who were to be questioned. Her Ladyship gave this explanation of the matters to be considered in such an application: [12] While the Alberta Rules of Court do not expressly limit the number of corporate witnesses an adverse party may question, Rule 5.19(a) allows the Court to limit the number. [13] As noted in Patel v Patel, 2011 ABQB 662 at para 38, the foundational Rules deal with fairness, justice, efficiency, economy and proportionality. As a result, the Court noted at para 43 that: [p]ermitting a party to avail him or herself of every step contemplated by the rules where there in no likelihood that the outcome of such steps will ultimately assist in resolving the matters, or where the potential benefits are disproportional to the efficiency and expense involved, is contrary to the purpose and intent of the rules. [14] The scope of questioning for discovery has been narrowed in the Rules from what is “relevant” to what is “relevant and material”. The Court of Appeal has cautioned, however, that: [a]t an interlocutory stage of proceedings, the Court should not measure counsels' proposed line of argument too finely; if counsel can disclose a rational strategy in which the disputed document plays a material part, that should be sufficient. Again it must be remembered that the purpose of the Rule was to avoid abusive, excessive, and unnecessarily expensive discovery, not to cut off legitimate line of inquiry: Weatherill Estate v Weatherill, 2003 ABQB 69, at paras 15-16. [15] Thus, the issue for the Court to grapple with is where to draw the line between legitimate and necessary questioning and questioning that is merely “fishing” for evidence without a reasonable basis or that has been proposed for illegitimate strategic reasons. [16] During questioning, a person is only required to answer relevant and material questions. A question is relevant and material only if the answer to that question could reasonably be expected either: a) to significantly help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings, or b) to ascertain evidence that could reasonably be expected to significantly help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings: Rules 5.2(1) and Rule 5.25 (1)(a). [17] Relevance is primarily determined with reference to the pleadings, while materiality relates to whether the information can help prove a fact in issue: Dow Chemical Canada Inc v Nova Chemicals Corp, 2014 ABCA 244 at para 17. [18] As noted at paras 19 and 21 of Dow Chemical, a case management judge is entitled to reject lines of pre-trial discovery that are unrealistic, speculative or without any air of reality, or where the expense involved is disproportionate to the likely benefits that will result. The same reasoning applies to requests to question witnesses generally. Justice Romaine concluded (at paragraph 47) that the proposed witnesses would not be produced for questioning because the party proposing to examine them had “not established that these proposed witnesses have any material and relevant information on the issues in this litigation.”

Location of Examination if Counsel Cannot Agree In cases like this one, where the solicitors and their clients all live in the same place, it is my opinion that if the solicitors cannot agree on where the examinations for discovery are to be held, they should be held at the Law Courts Building. MacQuarrie v. Bong (1995), 28 Alta. L.R. (3d) 142 (Master), at 144, per Master Quinn. Questioning by videoconference In Mostafa Altalibi Professional Corporation v. Lorne S. Kamelchuk Professional Corporation, 2022 ABCA 239, 2022 CarswellAlta 1746, additional reasons 2022 ABCA 364, a Master granted an order permitting questioning to be conducted by videoconference. A chambers judge upheld that order. The Court of Appeal agreed that the Court had the authority to issue such an order: [16] We agree with the chambers judge, that while the analysis in Sandhu related to questioning on affidavits, the situation with respect to questioning by videoconference is analogous and she had the authority to direct remote questioning and was correct to find that the master was also correct to find that the court had jurisdiction. [17] The chambers judge referred to Arconti v Smith, 2020 ONSC 2782, as being instructive and persuasive with respect to policy and general issues at play in respect of online discovery. We agree with Justice Myers' comments in Arcanti where he stated at paragraph 33: In my view, in 2020, use of readily available technology is part of the basic skillset required of civil litigators and courts. This is not new and, unlike the pandemic, did not arise on the sudden. However, the need for the court to operate during the pandemic has brought to the fore the availability of alternative processes and the imperative of technological competency. Efforts can and should be made to help people who remain uncomfortable to obtain any necessary training and education. Parties and counsel may require some delay to let one or both sides prepare to deal with unfamiliar surroundings.

sentences.text: Appropriate questions and objections

paragraphs.text: (1) During questioning, a person is required to answer only (a) relevant and material questions, and (b) questions in respect of which an objection is not upheld under subrule (2). (2) A party or a witness being questioned may object to an oral or written question during questioning but only for one or more of the following reasons: (a) privilege; (b) the question is not relevant and material; (c) the question is unreasonable or unnecessary; (d) any other ground recognized at law. (3) A corporate representative may object to an oral or written question during questioning on the basis that it would be unduly onerous for the corporate representative to inform himself or herself in the circumstances. (4) If an objection to a question cannot be resolved the Court must decide its validity. (5) After the questioning party has finished questioning a person, that person may be questioned by the party for whom the person is or may be a witness to explain, elaborate or provide context for an answer initially given. (6) Following answers to the explanatory, elaborative or contextual questions, the person may be questioned again about the person's answers.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.25:1 Rule 5.25 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.25. 1. Relevance and Materiality In Keyland Development Corp. v. Cochrane (Town), 2014 ABQB 458, 2014 CarswellAlta 1417, Justice Yamauchi set out a very useful summary of the law regarding questioning. His Lordship said, at paragraphs 25-47, and 54-55: 25 Rules r 5.25(1)(a) says that during questioning a person is required to answer only relevant and material questions. Rules r 5.2(1) says that a question is relevant and material only if the answer to the question could reasonably be expected significantly to help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings, or to ascertain evidence that could reasonably be expected significantly to help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings. 26 The issues set out in the pleadings determine a question's relevance. The Alberta Court of Appeal said the following in NAC Constructors Ltd. v Alberta Capital Region Wastewater Commission, 2006 ABCA 246, 412 AR 272, [NAC]: Oral examination for discovery is now confined to eliciting facts of primary relevance, that is, facts that are directly in issue, or of secondary relevance, that is, facts from which the existence of the primary facts may be directly inferred. Both primary and secondary relevance are determined by reference to the issues raised by the pleadings: NAC at para 12. [Emphasis added]. 27 But the Alberta Court of Appeal went on to set limits on how far the questioning could go, even when a party is seeking information that is of secondary relevance. It went on to say in the same paragraph: Questions seeking information that could reasonably be expected to lead to facts or records of secondary relevance (that is, questions asking for information that is only of tertiary relevance) need no longer be answered. 28 The court went on to define materiality as follows: In addition to being relevant within the meaning of Rule 186.1, information sought on discovery must be material, that is, be reasonably expected to “significantly” help determine one of more of the issues raised in the pleadings. The materiality of evidence refers to its pertinency or weight in relation to the issue it is adduced to prove: Black's Law Dictionary, (6th ed. 1990): NAC at para 13. 29 Where a party has the burden of proving a fact that is less amenable to direct proof, the court may permit the party to ask questions within a wider circle of materiality. In Weatherill (Estate) v. Fishing Expeditions The phrase “fishing expeditions” is frequently uttered when the topic of relevance is explored. Justice Slatter's discussion of the concept is very useful (see the reference to Tolko Industries Ltd. v. Railink Ltd., 2003 ABQB 349, 2003 CarswellAlta 559, 333 A.R. 270, 14 Alta. L.R. Baumann, 2019 ABQB 120, 2019 CarswellAlta 325: [45] The most quoted authority in Alberta about “fishing expeditions” is probably Franco v. Hackett, 2000 ABQB 241 (CanLII). At paragraph 34, Master Funduk said: I agree with Ms. Mah that the charts of Dr. Boldt are not relevant to this lawsuit. There are no gynaecological claims in this lawsuit. Mr. Hansen offers the usual submission that because the Plaintiff claims loss of income there might be something in Dr. Boldt's charts relevant to that. But the test is relevant and material. That now cuts out the old fishing expeditions. There is no fishing without first evidence that there are fish in the pond and a reasonable amount of fish. The Defendant has not satisfied me of that. Conjecture is not sufficient. [46] Master Funduk said “the test is relevant and material”. The Court of Appeal stated it another way in IMS Health Canada, Limited v. Information and Privacy Commissioner, 2005 ABCA 325 (CanLII) where it said at paragraph 53 that a “fishing expedition” would not be allowed unless there is “a valid reason for belief in the allegations underlying their attack”. [47] The point is that not every question that is not directly tied to a particular assertion in a pleading is improper “fishing”. Pre-trial questioning used to be called an “examination for discovery”. The name reflected that one of the purposes of the questioning is to “discover” what the other party's case is—its perspective on known facts, its knowledge about the allegations, its records of the events. Some “fishing” is inherent in the process. [48] As examples, questions such as “What is your education? What were your job responsibilities? Who else was present at the meeting? Did you make notes at the time? Was this the first time you drove this kind of vehicle?” are all questions that almost never arise out of the specific words in the pleadings, but are nonetheless relevant and material to understand the opposing party's perspective, knowledge, and the possible corroborating evidence from others, so as to allow the examining party what the disputes and arguments will be at trial. [49] The test for determining whether a question is proper, or whether the production of a record is required, is whether it is relevant and material. Rule 5.6 requires that an affidavit of records disclose all records that are relevant and material to the issues in the action and are or have been under the party's control. Rule 5.17 allows a party to ask questions about relevant and material information. [50] Even in Franco, Master Funduk did not say, “No fishing allowed.” He said, “There is no fishing without first evidence that there are fish in the pond and a reasonable amount of fish.” [51] That is effectively what the Court of Appeal said in IMS Health. [52] And that is what the Court said in Stealth Alarms. [53] Accordingly, not every question that cannot be tracked to specific wording in the pleading is a “fishing expedition”. The question is whether there is a proper basis for the question given the dispute. When the claim is that the defendant has embarked on a campaign of defamation, and there is some factual basis to support that claim, Stealth Alarms tells us that questions going beyond the persons already identified as having heard or read the communications is appropriate. 5. Repetitive and abusive questions have never been allowed: Rozak (Estate), 2011 ABQB 239 (CanLII) at para 31. Such questions are “time-wasting, pointless and a violation of the Foundational Rules”: Allan at para 65; Milavsky at para 183. [7] There are recognized exceptions when re-asking a question may be appropriate, and counsel does have a right to reframe or rephrase questions in order to obtain meaningful admissions: Allan at para 65; Braden v Knisley Estate, 2010 SKQB 335 (CanLII) at para 43. Re-asking a question is acceptable when: (1) the question has not actually been answered despite being asked, (2) new information is revealed that calls for re-visiting previous testimony, and (3) counsel is simply reminding a witness of a topic previously discussed and confirming a previous answer: Milavsky at paras 180–182. Information not Known to the Witness [8] In Wright v Schultz, [1992] 135 AR 58 (CA) at para 25, the Alberta Court of Appeal determined that an individual examined for discovery must only inform themselves on matters within the knowledge of anyone under their control, including employees and agents. There is no obligation to attest to information outside their knowledge, or to inform themselves on matters outside their control: BN v Canada (AG), 1998 ABQB 786 (CanLII) at para 12. [9] This Court confirmed that a witness's requirement to inform themselves on cross-examination on an affidavit is the same as on cross-examination for discovery in Canadian Western Bank v Alberta, 2003 ABQB 254 (CanLII) at para 18. [10] One way to attempt to elicit information that is outside the knowledge of a witness is by posing hypothetical questions. While hypothetical questions are not improper in themselves, they cannot become speculative, unrealistic or lack an air of reality: Maple Trade Finance Inc v Euler Hermes Canada, 2015 NSSC 37 (CanLII) at para 47; Dow Chemical Canada ULC v Nova Chemical Corporation, 2014 ABCA 244 (CanLII) at para 21. In asking hypothetical questions, counsel must not (i) go beyond the pleadings (here, Originating Application) to find a claim or defence that has not been raised; (ii) ask the witness a patently overbroad or vague question; or (iii) ask the witness to comment on the actions or failures of other persons: Maple Trade at para 47. Irrelevant Information [11] Rule 3.13 of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010 governs who counsel may question on an affidavit for an Originating Application. In his commentary on this rule, Judge Fradsham notes that the examination under this rule may be “as searching and thorough” as examination on discovery; however, it must not “extend to matters wholly immaterial and irrelevant to the affidavit”: Judge Allan A Fradsham, Alberta Rules of Court Annotated 2019 (Toronto: Thomson Reuters, 2018) at 119). [12] The Alberta Court of Appeal in Dow Chemical at paragraph 17 indicated that “relevance is primarily determined by the pleadings”. When a matter proceeds by Originating Application, there is no opportunity for the respondent to file a document equivalent to a Statement of Defence. However, that respondent, in this case Ms. Moser, is still entitled to raise anything relevant and material to the claim advanced in the Originating Application, potentially capturing the “whole lawsuit”: Gill v 735458 Alberta Inc, 2003 ABQB 501 (CanLII) at paras 16, 35; Alberta (AG) v Alberta Power (2000) Ltd, 2017 ABQB 195 (CanLII) at para 26. [13] Thus, when questioning on an affidavit in support of an application, questions relevant to the underlying application are permitted, and if they are refused, the Court may order that they be answered: Rozak at para 30. But issues relevant to the application are not confined to the “four corners of the affidavit”: Dow Chemical Canada ULC v Shell Chemicals Canada Ltd, 2008 ABQB 671 (CanLII) at para 7. Cross examination may be “searching, thorough and not bound strictly to the material set out in … the Affidavit, but is limited to issues arising from the Affidavit as they relate to the motion”: Bond Street Properties Inc v Alberta Permit Pro, 2010 ABQB 416 (CanLII) at para 45 citing Colortech Painting and Decorating Ltd v Toh, 2000 ABQB 814 (CanLII) at para 26. [14] In order to determine what information or documents are relevant in this matter, this Court must review the issues in the underlying Originating Application: Rozak at para 32. … Solicitor-Client Privilege [19] Solicitor-client privilege attaches to confidential communications between a lawyer and their client for the purpose of seeking legal advice: Descôteaux v Mierzwinski, 1982 CanLII 22 (SCC), [1982] 1 SCR 860 at 872-3; AARC Society v Sparks, 2018 ABCA 177 (CanLII) at para 2. [20] This privilege extends to in-house counsel acting in their capacity as lawyers by giving advice or seeking instructions: NEP Canada v MEC OP LLC, 2013 ABQB 540 (CanLII) at para 25. Whether the privilege attaches to a communication with in-house counsel depends on: (a) the nature of the relationship, (b) the subject matter of the advice, and (c) the circumstances in which the advice is sought and rendered: R v Campbell, 1999 CanLII 676 (SCC), [1999] 1 SCR 565 at para 50. [21] This privilege receives significant protection during the discovery process. Where a party asserts privilege over a document, the “obligation to provide sufficient information to indicate how a record fits within the claimed privilege does not require a degree of particularity that would defeat the privilege”: Canadian Natural Resources Ltd v ShawCor Ltd, 2014 ABCA 289 (CanLII) at para 56. Solicitor-Client Privilege and Directors [22] When a corporation obtains legal advice, control over the privilege rests with its officers and directors: Adam M Dodek, Solicitor-Client Privilege (Markham: LexisNexis, 2014) at 410. Thus, a Board of Directors as an entity enjoys “the right of unfettered access to legal advice provided to the corporation”: ibid at 411 [23] However, this right is truncated when a Director is in an adversarial position to a corporation. In support of this proposition, the parties pointed this Court to two American authorities: Kalisman v Friedman, 2013 Del Ch LEXIS 100, 2013 WL 1668205; Chambers v Gold Medal Bakery Inc, 464 Mass 383 (Mass SC), 983 NE (2d) 683. This statement of the law has also received support in Canadian authorities. For example, in Livent Inc, Re, [1999] OJ No 5981 at para 4, 1999 CarswellOnt 4383 aff'd 2000 CarswellOnt 1890 (CA): I am of the view that, in a situation where a corporation is engaged in litigation with one or more of its directors, the right of those directors to access corporate records provided by the OBCA must be subject to any solicitor client privilege or litigation privilege of that corporation with respect to matters at issue in the litigation in the same manner as the right provided to a party by the Rules of Civil Procedure to disclosure of all documents having a semblance of relevance to the litigation is subject to such privileges. To hold otherwise would lead to the ludicrous result that the director engaged in litigation with the corporation would not be entitled to access in his capacity as a litigant, but would be entitled to access in his capacity as a director, thereby indirectly negating the solicitor client privilege or litigation privilege of the corporation. [emphasis added] [24] Similarly, in Wang v British Columbia Medical Association, 2011 BCSC 1658 (CanLII) at para 71, the Court found that documents were protected by privilege from the plaintiff after she was clearly in conflict with the Association because she had been cited for a breach of the code of conduct and had retained counsel.
