sentences.text: Commentary § 5.25:1 Rule 5.25 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta.
Reg.
Relevance and Materiality In Keyland Development Corp. v.
Cochrane (Town), 2014 ABQB 458, 2014 CarswellAlta 1417, Justice Yamauchi set out a very useful summary of the law regarding questioning.
His Lordship said, at paragraphs 25-47, and 54-55: 25 Rules r 5.25(1)(a) says that during questioning a person is required to answer only relevant and material questions.

Rules r 5.2(1) says that a question is relevant and material only if the answer to the question could reasonably be expected significantly to help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings, or to ascertain evidence that could reasonably be expected significantly to help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings.
26 The issues set out in the pleadings determine a question's relevance.

The Alberta Court of Appeal said the following in NAC Constructors Ltd. v Alberta Capital Region Wastewater Commission, 2006 ABCA 246, 412 AR 272, [NAC]: Oral examination for discovery is now confined to eliciting facts of primary relevance, that is, facts that are directly in issue, or of secondary relevance, that is, facts from which the existence of the primary facts may be directly inferred.
Both primary and secondary relevance are determined by reference to the issues raised by the pleadings: NAC at para 12.
[Emphasis added].
27 But the Alberta Court of Appeal went on to set limits on how far the questioning could go, even when a party is seeking information that is of secondary relevance.

It went on to say in the same paragraph: Questions seeking information that could reasonably be expected to lead to facts or records of secondary relevance (that is, questions asking for information that is only of tertiary relevance) need no longer be answered.

28 The court went on to define materiality as follows: In addition to being relevant within the meaning of Rule 186.1, information sought on discovery must be material, that is, be reasonably expected to “significantly” help determine one of more of the issues raised in the pleadings.
The materiality of evidence refers to its pertinency or weight in relation to the issue it is adduced to prove: Black's Law Dictionary, (6th ed.
1990): NAC at para 13.
29 Where a party has the burden of proving a fact that is less amenable to direct proof, the court may permit the party to ask questions within a wider circle of materiality.
In Weatherill (Estate) v.

Weatherill, 2003 ABQB 69 at para 16, 337 AR 180, Slatter J, as he then was, stated as follows: There are some facts that can only be proven by essentially eliminating all the competing scenarios, thereby leaving the fact in issue as the sole logical inference.
When a state of mind is in issue, it can generally only be proven by demonstrating a pattern of conduct of the person whose state of mind it is.
In deciding whether a particular document is material, one must take a very pragmatic view, viewing the situation from the perspective of the party who must prove the fact in question.

At an interlocutory stage of proceedings, the Court should not measure counsels' proposed line of argument too finely; if counsel can disclose a rational strategy in which the disputed document plays a material part, that should be sufficient.
Again it must be remembered that the purpose of the Rule was to avoid abusive, excessive, and unnecessarily expensive discovery, not to cut off legitimate lines of inquiry.
[Emphasis added].
30 HMQ argues that the word “document” in the emphasized portion of this quotation may also refer to a question.
This Court agrees.

31 In Tolko Industries Ltd v Railink Ltd, 2003 ABQB 349 at para 7, 33 AR 270, Slatter J, as he then was, again explains relevance and materiality: Counsel also referred to the decision of Master Funduk in Franco v.
Hackett 2000 ABQB 241 (CanLII), (2000), 262 A.R.
127 at para.
But the test is relevant and material.
That now cuts out the old fishing expeditions.
There is no fishing without first evidence that there are fish in the pond and a reasonable amount of fish.
Defendant has not satisfied me of that.
Conjecture is not sufficient.
This statement has caused counsel in subsequent cases to embark on all sorts of piscatorial analogies.
The metaphor is helpful if one remembers that with respect to the scope of discovery of the parties the question of “whether there are fish” is determined by the pleadings.
If one of the parties pleads that there are or are not fish, then that is determinative of the issue as far as discovery goes.
As to whether there are “a reasonable amount of fish”, that relates to materiality.

Rule 186 says that there are a reasonable amount of fish if there are enough to significantly help determine one or more issues, or to ascertain evidence that can significantly help determine an issue.
Under the new Rule fishing expeditions are still permitted if they fall within that test.
32 During questioning, issues of relevance and materiality must be assessed separately and apart from determinations as to admissibility and weight, which are issues properly disposed of at trial.

Thus, the person conducting the questioning enjoys fairly wide latitude when posing their questions, as such questions may be proper even if the answer to it might offend the rules of evidence: Devon Canada Corp v TransCanada Power Services Ltd (cob TransCanada Power LP), 2006 ABQB 637 [Devon Canada] at para 13 summarizing the Alberta Court of Appeal decision in Hepworth v Canadian Equestrian Federation, 2000 ABCA 327, 277 AR 138.

In Devon Canada, McIntyre J went on to say the following: The Court stated that all pleadings are to be reviewed, but the surrounding circumstances may be relevant to give context to contracts, and that the validity of the issues raised in the pleadings should be left in the trial judge.
Further, the Court once more noted that the parties have been given wide latitude in asking questions on discovery, citing Tremco Inc. v.
Gienow Building Products Ltd., 2000 ABCA 105 (CanLII), [2000] A.J.
No.
366; 2000 ABCA 105, a case that preceded the 1999 amendment.
33 Rules r 5.22 provides that questioning may be conducted under oath, orally or by way of written questions.
Of course, Rules rr 5.2(1) and 5.25(1)(a) apply to both oral and written questions.

If the person being questioned discovers that their answer to a question was incorrect or misleading, or the answer becomes incorrect or misleading as a result of new information, they must correct their answer through an affidavit: Rules r 5.27.
This is consistent with the decision of Wachowich ACJ, as he then was, in Esso Resources Canada Ltd v Stearns Catalytic Ltd
(1993), 20 Alta LR
(3d) 320 (QB) [Esso], where he said the following: Clearly, the purpose of examinations for discovery is to discover all the facts within the other parties' knowledge.

Consistent with that purpose the corporate officer may advise the examining party that it has contrary, inconsistent or supplemental information and the nature of the evidence which supports that information.

The corporate officer is thereby advising the examining party of the case to be met in complying with his general duty to disclose any inconsistent or supplementary information he has obtained through reasonable inquiry, if requested to do so: Esso at 325.

34 Earlier, he said the following: Practically speaking, a corporate officer who has had excerpts from the discovery of employees or former employees of the corporation made available to him will usually be under an obligation to acknowledge that those excerpts form part of the information of the corporation.

This practical reality is not equivalent to the defendant's submission that this Court is therefore ordering the corporate officer to answer in a prescribed manner and acting outside its jurisdiction.
The corporate officer certainly has the ability to append to this admission a qualification.
Such a qualification should have a factual basis and the facts relied upon should be clearly identified by the corporate officer as part of his answer.

This is only proper as the officer is under a general duty to disclose to the examining party any inconsistent, contrary or otherwise additional information he has obtained through reasonable inquiry into the matters in issue if requested to do so: Esso at 312.
35 However, the corporate officer has no obligation to provide a confirmatory response.
In Western Canadian Place Ltd v Con-Force Products Ltd (1996), 39 Alta LR (3d) 432, 188 AR 73 (QB) [Con-Force], McMahon J said the following: The real issue then in Esso v.

Stearns, supra, was when and how the witness being examined could put on the record qualifying information—that is, facts that were contrary to or inconsistent with the answers already given by the employee or ex-employee.
The case did not deal with the obligation—as opposed to the right—of the witness being examined to provide general confirmatory information.
In my view, there is no such obligation.

A broad request that the officer being examined inform himself and disclose all information on a particular subject and in the corporate party's possession, whether contrary to another employee's answers or not, places an unreasonable burden on the witness. … An officer has an obligation to respond fully.

If, after informing himself, he has information which qualifies his answer—in the sense of being contrary to or inconsistent with the answers already given—then he is obliged, if asked, to give that qualification.
If he is not asked for the qualification, then his right to impose that qualification upon his answer is dealt with by the decisions in Esso v.
Stearns.
I do not mean to say that merely because the answer to a specific question might confirm another answer, such question is improper.

To use an example which arose during argument, if employee A has said that the temperature at a given time was 3 degrees; and the officer has said that the company has no contrary information, he can nevertheless be asked specifically whether employee B knew what the temperature was and if so, what he said it was: Con-Force at paras 8, 11-12.
36 What concerned McMahon J in Con-Force was the compendious nature of the demand placed on the party who was being questioned.
The breadth of the information that the questioning party was seeking was, to McMahon J's mind, overly broad.

37 If the party questioning is of the view that the answers to the written questions or the answers to the follow-up written or follow-up oral questions are unsatisfactory, it may, pursuant to Rules r 5.28(3), apply to the court for an order allowing it to conduct oral or further oral questioning or compelling the party being questioned to respond to the written questions.
38 Persons who are being questioned must inform themselves of the information that forms the subject of the litigation; even if that means making inquiries of others.
In Wright v Schultz (1992), 135 AR 58 at 63 (CA) [Wright], Hetherington JA said the following: Must the appellant seek information from others?

In my view an individual who is examined for discovery must inform himself of matters within the knowledge of anyone over whom he has control and he must inform himself of matters within the knowledge of his employees and agents.
See also McLean v Canadian Pacific Railway
(1916), 10 WWR 949 at 951 (Alta CA); Tiedemann v Basiuk
(1977), 4 Alta LR
(2d) 12 at para 5 (QB); Canadian Utilities Ltd v Mannix Ltd et al
(1959), 29 WWR (NS) 289 (Alta CA); Turkawski v 738675 Alberta Ltd
39 Questioning is a factual journey, not an evidentiary one.
The factual journey must relate to the pleadings.
In Can-Air Services Ltd v British Aviation Insurance Co
(1988), 63 Alta LR

(2d) 61 (CA) [Can-Air] at 64, 67, Côté JA said the following: An examining lawyer could properly say, “Paragraph 4(b) of your Statement of Claim alleges that the driver was impaired by alcohol at the time of the collision.
Tell me all the facts about that impairment which you know or must properly inform yourself of”.
There both the pleadings and the question are factual, so the question is proper.
If the questioner instead asks “On what facts do you rely for paragraph 4(b)”, the witness's lawyer may properly object.
Then the questioner must decide whether he wants the opposing party's strategy or evidence or law (which he cannot get), or whether he simply wants facts (which he can).
If he wants facts, he must rephrase his question, e.g., along the lines suggested.
(If the paragraph in question pleads law or a legal conclusion, then such rephrasing may not cure the question.).
40 Rules r 5.30 deals with undertakings that a person provides during questioning.
Rules r 5.30(2) states that further questioning may be undertaken “on the answer given or record provided.” It does not open the person up to further general questioning.
In other words, the questioning must be focused on the response to the undertaking.
Certainly, it is within the power of this Court to allow a party to conduct further questioning that goes beyond the undertakings.

For it to make this allowance, the party seeking the relief must show “special circumstances” to justify its request: Taylor v Alberta (Administrator, Motor Vehicle Accident Claims Act), 2005 ABQB 612, 385 AR 161, or where justice so requires it: Boulianne v Two Hills (County) No 21
41 In Senechal v.

Muskoka (Municipality), [2005] OJ No 1406, 2005 CarswellOnt 1414 (Master) [Senechal], Master MacLeod said that “undertakings are an acknowledgment that the question is a proper one and a promise to obtain and provide the answer.” He then went on to say the following: Generally speaking, had … the answer to the undertaking been available, not only would the answer have been given under oath as part of the transcript but the examining party would have been entitled to ask appropriate follow up questions as part of the examination.
Arguably then an answer that genuinely gives rise to follow up questions should give rise to a right to complete the oral discovery as if the question has been answered: Senechal at para 5.

42 He noted, however, that a party does not have an absolute right to pose follow-up questions and, in particular, a court is “not required to order reattendance and a follow up examination simply to allow the sterile exercise of a right if it serves no purpose”: Senechal at para 6.

Master McLeod went on to summarize a non-exhaustive list of principles he gleaned from the various cases to which he referred as follows: • As a general principle a party giving undertakings or answering refusals may be required to re-attend to complete the discovery by giving the answers under oath and answering appropriate follow up questions.

A party being examined may not compel the examining party to accept answers in writing simply by refusing to answer questions or by giving undertakings. • On the other hand, the court will not automatically make an order for follow up discovery if it serves no useful purpose.

Examples in which an order may not be appropriate would be cases in which a full and complete written response has been given to a simple question, in which the answer demonstrates that the question was not relevant or in which the parties have agreed that written answers will suffice. • The court will generally make such an order if it appears necessary in order to fulfill the purposes of discovery.

Examples of situations in which an order would be appropriate are situations in which the answers appear cursory or incomplete, where they give rise to apparently relevant follow up questions that have not been asked, if newly produced documents require explanation, or the discovery transcript supplemented by the answers will not be understandable or useable at trial. • Even if answers do appear to require follow up, the court has discretion to order answers in writing or to decline to order further examination where it appears the cost or the onerous nature of what is proposed outweighs the possible benefit or where for any other reason it appears unjust to make such an order.
Such discretion should be exercised only if the interests of justice require it: Senechal at para 7.
[Emphasis added].
He concludes by saying that, “[t]he point is that discovery rights are subject to court supervision and are not absolute rights”: Senechal at para 8.
See also Blais v Toronto Area Transit Operating Authority, 2011 ONSC 1880 at para 63, 105 OR (3d) 575.
43 The limits on questioning following the compliance with undertakings was further addressed in International Minerals & Chemical Corp (Canada) Ltd v Commonwealth Insurance Co

(1992), 104 Sask R 275 at para 21 (QB), where Halvorson J said the following: Where a party has responded to an undertaking, the examiner on a resumed discovery may pose questions respecting the response whether or not the response has been challenged.
This does not equate to an examination on areas neglected in the original discovery.
[Emphasis added].
44 In a similar vein, Roslak J said the following in Saskatchewan Government Insurance v Treen, 1988 CarswellAlta 934 at para 7, 11 ACWS

(3d) 249 (QB): … the questions in issue are relevant to the issues raised in this case and flow logically from the answers given upon the undertakings provided at the previous Examination for Discovery …[Emphasis added].
45 Nor can a party clothe its questions as follow-up questions, when the party being questioned has already responded to the question or the answers can be found in previous production.
In Kinch v Walden, 2011 ONSC 2791, 202 ACWS

(3d) 263 [Kinch], Reilly J said the following: …[T]he questions they wish answered are simply clarification of information the defendants already have from the productions supplied … initially or pursuant to the original examinations for discovery.
The defendants have all the information they need in my view, to inquire into these issues at trial.

Their substantive rights are not impacted by the issues they raise: Kinch at para 18 46 Of course, the party who provided the undertaking must comply with the undertaking they provided during questioning.

If they choose to be evasive or “cute” by not answering the question, not responding or saying that a document in issue speaks for itself, the court will require that party to respond to the question in writing or through further questioning: Desilets Estate v Daon Development Corp, 1989 CarswellAlta 962, 16 ACWS
(3d) 311 (QB Master).

Furthermore, if the undertaking is unqualified, the party giving the undertaking must comply with it strictly, without unilaterally qualifying it: Litemor Distributors (Edmonton) Ltd v Midwest Furnishings & Supplies Ltd, 2002 ABQB 713 at para 7 (Master).

47 If it is clear from the record, and from the nature of the undertaking, that the questioning party could go no further with their questioning until they obtained compliance with the undertaking, the court might be willing to allow it to conduct further questioning (or clarification of the response to the written interrogatory): Olson v Golden Giant Employee's Assn, 1999 CarswellOnt 4552 paras 16-17 (Sup Ct Jus)
Ennis v Young, 1986 CarswellOnt 3811 at paras 2 and 4, 4 WDCP 546 (Sup Ct Master). … 54 The test for production is relevance and materiality.
During questioning, a party must answer all relevant questions posed by an adverse party.
The only exception is where the adverse party asks for privileged information.
Confidentiality agreements are not a basis for a category/class of privilege recognized at law.
See Jardine Lloyd Thompson Canada Inc v Western Oil Sands Inc, 2006 ABCA 18, 13 BLR (4th) 1, 380 AR 121.

55 If relevant and material information in an action is not protected by a particular category/class of privilege, the information may nonetheless be privileged only if it meets the test for case-by-case privilege developed by Professor Wigmore. … Another useful summary of the law governing questioning, including the concepts of relevance and materiality, is found in Brookdale International v.
Crescent Point Energy, 2023 ABKB 120, 2023 CarswellAlta 525 at paras.
2. “Facts” distinguished from “evidence” In CNOOC Petroleum North America ULC v.

ITP SA, 2024 ABKB 639, Associate Chief Justice Nixon said: [11] There is an important distinction in discovery between facts and evidence. “Facts, which enable a party to know what the case is, are discoverable.
Evidence, which enables a party to know how the case will be proved, is not […]”: Brookdale International [Brookdale International v.
Cresecent Point Energy, 2023 ABKB 120] at para 22.
Questions about a witness's understanding In PetroFrontier Corp. v.
Macquarie Capital Markets Canada Ltd., 2021 ABQB 54, 2021 CarswellAlta 266, affirmed 2022 ABCA 136, leave to appeal refused 2023 CarswellAlta 58 (S.C.C.), Justice G.A.

Campbell said: [60] In general, questions about a witness's understanding or what they thought about their obligations are not relevant or material to what those obligations were or whether they were breached.
This is because the law considers parties' words and conduct as objectively construed, without regard for their subjective views: Eli Lilly & Co v Novopharm Inc, [1998] 2 SCR 129, 1998 CanLII 791
Bhasin v Hrynew, 2013 ABCA 98 at paras 26-27
Gainers Inc. v Pocklington Holdings Ltd., 2000 ABCA 151.
[61] But questioning is about facts.

[62] Questions about a witness's understanding, expectation or opinion that they held at a specific time in the past are questions of fact: Opron Construction Co. v Alberta, [1988] AJ No 232, 1988 CanLII 3469 (ABQB).
[63] Further, the state of mind of a witness is a fact.
The scope of questioning in this circumstance was discussed by Slatter, J.

(as he then was) in Weatherill, at para 16: There are some facts that can only be proven by essentially eliminating all the competing scenarios, thereby leaving the fact in issue as the sole logical inference.
When a state of mind is in issue, it can generally only be proven by demonstrating a pattern of conduct of the person whose state of mind it is.
In deciding whether a particular document is material, one must take a very pragmatic view, viewing the situation from the perspective of the party who must prove the fact in question.

At an interlocutory stage of proceedings, the Court should not measure counsels' proposed line of argument too finely; if counsel can disclose a rational strategy in which the disputed document plays a material part, that should be sufficient.
Again it must be remembered that the purpose of the Rule was to avoid abusive, excessive, and unnecessarily expensive discovery, not to cut off legitimate lines of inquiry.

[64] Questions regarding what a witness did, why they did it, or why they did not do it, and whether at the time they believed they were right in what they did or did not do may demonstrate that the party knew what its obligations were and deliberately acted contrary to them, making this line of questioning relevant and material: Romanow, at para 29.

As Master Robertson stated in Romanow, at para 40: … But in many cases the understanding that a party had when it did the things in question is germane to the issue pled because the party's state of mind is in issue, and the party's current understanding may be relevant as well.
[65] Thus, in certain circumstances, what a witness thought, understood or expected at the time of the events in issue are facts that may well be relevant and material.
The relevant query is whether the question can help determine any of the issues raised in the pleadings.
[66] Questioning is to seek facts, not law.
Questions about conclusions of law are not proper questions.

A witness's view about the legal effect of a legal requirement or provision, such as the meaning of a provision in a contract, is irrelevant because that is the domain of legal argument, judicial interpretation and determination.
However, it is permissible to ask a witness to provide their understanding of the facts represented in a document or legal circumstance, which is neither an opinion nor interpretation.
[67] I accept that questions regarding opinions, understandings, and expectations held at the time are questions seeking facts and are proper and permissible.
However, the general principles of relevance and materiality articulated above must still be met in order to find that a question must be answered.
Fishing Expeditions The phrase “fishing expeditions” is frequently uttered when the topic of relevance is explored.
Justice Slatter's discussion of the concept is very useful (see the reference to Tolko Industries Ltd. v.
Railink Ltd., 2003 ABQB 349, 2003 CarswellAlta 559, 333 A.R.
L.R.
No.
529 as set out by Justice Yamauchi in Keyland Development Corp. v.
Cochrane (Town) in the annotation “Relevance and Materiality” above).
Master Robertson has also discussed “fishing expeditions” in his decision in Callidus Capital Corporation v.
Baumann, 2019 ABQB 120, 2019 CarswellAlta 325: [45] The most quoted authority in Alberta about “fishing expeditions” is probably Franco v.
Hackett, 2000 ABQB 241 (CanLII).
At paragraph 34, Master Funduk said: I agree with Ms.
Mah that the charts of Dr.
Boldt are not relevant to this lawsuit.
There are no gynaecological claims in this lawsuit.
Mr.
Hansen offers the usual submission that because the Plaintiff claims loss of income there might be something in Dr.
Boldt's charts relevant to that.
But the test is relevant and material.
That now cuts out the old fishing expeditions.
There is no fishing without first evidence that there are fish in the pond and a reasonable amount of fish.
The Defendant has not satisfied me of that.
Conjecture is not sufficient.
[46] Master Funduk said “the test is relevant and material”.
The Court of Appeal stated it another way in IMS Health Canada, Limited v.

Information and Privacy Commissioner, 2005 ABCA 325 (CanLII) where it said at paragraph 53 that a “fishing expedition” would not be allowed unless there is “a valid reason for belief in the allegations underlying their attack”.
[47] The point is that not every question that is not directly tied to a particular assertion in a pleading is improper “fishing”.
Pre-trial questioning used to be called an “examination for discovery”.

The name reflected that one of the purposes of the questioning is to “discover” what the other party's case is—its perspective on known facts, its knowledge about the allegations, its records of the events.
Some “fishing” is inherent in the process.
[48] As examples, questions such as “What is your education?
What were your job responsibilities?
Who else was present at the meeting?
Did you make notes at the time?

Was this the first time you drove this kind of vehicle?” are all questions that almost never arise out of the specific words in the pleadings, but are nonetheless relevant and material to understand the opposing party's perspective, knowledge, and the possible corroborating evidence from others, so as to allow the examining party what the disputes and arguments will be at trial.
[49] The test for determining whether a question is proper, or whether the production of a record is required, is whether it is relevant and material.
Rule 5.6 requires that an affidavit of records disclose all records that are relevant and material to the issues in the action and are or have been under the party's control.
Rule 5.17 allows a party to ask questions about relevant and material information.

[50] Even in Franco, Master Funduk did not say, “No fishing allowed.” He said, “There is no fishing without first evidence that there are fish in the pond and a reasonable amount of fish.” [51] That is effectively what the Court of Appeal said in IMS Health.
[52] And that is what the Court said in Stealth Alarms.
[53] Accordingly, not every question that cannot be tracked to specific wording in the pleading is a “fishing expedition”.
The question is whether there is a proper basis for the question given the dispute.

When the claim is that the defendant has embarked on a campaign of defamation, and there is some factual basis to support that claim, Stealth Alarms tells us that questions going beyond the persons already identified as having heard or read the communications is appropriate.
Use of Rule 5.25(5) to Qualify an Opinion Assume that the representative of a corporate party offers an opinion with which the corporation does not agree.
Rules 207 and 214(4), now Rules 5.25 and 5.31(3), provide a solution.
If the opinion of the selected officer given at discovery is rejected by the defendant then the defendant's concern is seen.
It may be resolved by the defendant calling the selected officer at trial to explain or by the defendant examining him under R.
207 and asking him if his opinion was accepted by the defendant or relied upon by the defendant or whatever.
If the answer of the selected officer is that the defendant did not accept his opinion (or whatever) then his answer may be the subject of an application under R.
214(4) should the plaintiff read in the selected officer's opinion as part of his discovery.
Such an application will show that, while the selected officer held a particular opinion, that opinion was not held or was otherwise rejected by the defendant.
Opron Construction Co. v.
Alberta (1988), 59 Alta.
L.R.
This decision was affirmed on the issue (1990), 71 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 28 (C.A.), at 37, per Côté J.: In the first place, when the officer gives his opinion on discovery, he or his counsel may make it clear that it is just his personal view.
If the corporation has not adopted it (or rejects it), either can say so.
I will not elaborate on what words or devices they might use.
As the chambers judge points out, the corporation may use R.
207 on re-examining the officer, and R.
214(4) on reading in connected answers at trial.
Objectionable Questions (i) Interpreting a record In an examination for discovery, examining counsel read to the witness a paragraph from a contract.

He then asked: “Do you see that?” The witness said: “I understood the sentences as you read it.” Examining counsel then provided an interpretation of the paragraph and asked the witness: “Is that correct?” An objection was taken to the question on the grounds that it requested a legal opinion of the witness.
The court agreed and said: If Mr.
Wolinsky is merely asking the officer to literally read back what article 5.01 says he is wasting everybody's time.
The officer is not taking a reading skill test.
If the officer is being asked what the article means that is a matter of interpretation and the interpretation of a document is a matter of law: Côté, An Introduction to the Law of Contract, pp.
The officer's view of what article 5.01 means is irrelevant.
It is not any the less a question of law because the question is asked at discovery, not trial… The officer is not asked a fact.
If the officer is merely being asked to literally read aloud what the article says, what is the point of it?
The agreement is an exhibit in the examination.
If the officer is being asked what the article means (its effect) he is being asked to interpret it.
Alberta (Provincial Treasurer) v.
National Bank of Canada (1995), 172 A.R.
282 (Master), at 285-86, per Master Funduk.

(ii) “Are you suggesting?” questions If questions, though not clearly stated as such, are questions that in effect request an opinion in law, then they are objectionable. … if the questions are “in effect” questions of law they are not permissible… sometimes questioners try to evade the rule in a certain fashion.
Questions that are questions of law can be dressed up to look like something else… Can-Air[Can-Air Services Ltd. v.
British Aviation Insurance Co.
L.R.
(2d) 61 (C.A.)] pulls that kind of example from R. v.
Baldwin[see [1925] All E.R.
Rep.
Can-Air says that not all trial rules of cross-examination apply to discovery, but the quote “reminds us of the logical and practical implications of the rule restricting questions to facts”.
The problem with Mr.
Wolinsky's submission that he is just seeking to have the officer clarify earlier answers is twofold.
First, the questions are in substance in the “are you suggesting?” category.
This is what Baldwin says, p.
404 [All E.R.]: There is a further matter involved here which goes far beyond the present case, and, it may be, beyond criminal cases.
One so often hears questions put to witnesses by counsel which are really in the nature of an invitation to an argument.

One hears, for instance, such questions as this: ‘I suggest to you that …’ or ‘Is your evidence to be taken as suggesting that…?’ If the witness were a prudent person, he would say, with the highest degree of politeness: ‘What you suggest is no business of mine.
I am not here to make any suggestions at all.
I am here only to answer relevant questions.

What are the conclusions to be drawn from my answers is not for me, and as for suggestions, I venture to leave those to others.’ An answer of that kind requires, no doubt, some sense and self-restraint and experience.
In this case what is the difference between “are you saying that …” and “are you suggesting that …” I do not see any.
Second, the officer is being asked to make a conclusion even though the questions are dressed up in different pants. “The consumer does not see a tax.
Therefore there is no tax.
Right?”“You do not see it.
Therefore it does not exist.
Right?” “Because” questions are often questions that call for the witness to make a conclusion.
The officer is not asked “does the consumer see a tax?” or “do you see a tax”.
What follows after that, the “because” part, turns them into questions asking the officer for conclusions.
Leaving aside expert witnesses, witnesses should not be asked questions which call for conclusions based on facts …Alberta (Provincial Treasurer) v.
National Bank of Canada (1995), 172 A.R.
282 (Master), at 288-89, per Master Funduk.
(iii) “On what facts do you rely” questions See the annotation to R.
5.17: “Questions Regarding Pleadings”.
Objections relating to the production of records In Allen v.
Telfer, 2018 ABQB 876, 2018 CarswellAlta 2462 (Master), Master Robertson discussed the proper way to object to producing records.
After referring to the directions found in foundational rules 1.2(2)(b)
(d), and

(e), and 1.2(3)(b), the learned Master said: [6] These directions follow the stated purpose of the rules, which is set out in rule 1.2(1) thus: “The purpose of these rules is to provide a means by which claims can be fairly and justly resolved in or by a court process in a timely and cost-effective way.” [7] In my view the objections to questions and the objections to undertakings must be looked at with this in mind.
[8] I make this observation in part because some of the questions were objected to, or undertakings declined, on the basis of the precise way the question was asked.
Senior counsel will often discuss the question asked and an agreement is reached as to how it may appropriately be addressed when there is some valid objection to part of the information requested.

[9] That is, if the objection is to produce an entire document, where only a few pages of it are relevant, or the request is to produce an entire file, where a portion of it is relevant, counsel for the witness being examined must reflect on the fact that if a portion of the those records are producible, they should have been produced in the first place.

[10] Accordingly, it is not an appropriate objection to say, “The request is too broad, therefore I need not produce any of the records sought.” Technically, the objection could be made that the request for production is too broad, and then the party being examined could provide a revised affidavit of records at a later date listing the records that are proper to produce, but that may simply delay matters.
When further records are going to be produced, the opposing party is entitled to examine on them.
Why not focus on what will be produced, see if an agreement can be reached as to the parameters, and give the appropriate undertaking?
That would seem to be the best way to comply with rule 2.2(d) in the circumstances.
Four common objections to questions In Real Estate Council of Alberta v.
Moser, 2019 ABQB 106, Madam Justice Ho had before her a series of questions put to witnesses at a questioning, and to which counsel had objected for various reasons.

In her ruling, Justice Ho gave a helpful summary of the law relating to each of the objections: [3] The parties submitted an itemized table which elaborates on each undertaking and question requiring this Court's direction.
The parties agreed to a categorization of the outstanding questions and undertakings based on the objections raised by RECA's counsel to the individual undertaking or question.
The four categories are: 1.
Asked and answered; 2.
Information not known to the witness; 3.
Lack of relevance; and 4.

Solicitor-client privilege. … [5] The applicable law relevant to the four categories is summarized below. … Asked and Answered [6] The objection of “asked and answered” is a valid objection where the question has actually been both asked and answered: Milavsky v Lashyn, 2016 ABQB 410 (CanLII) at para 180.
Assessing whether the objection is raised correctly involves considering the abuse that results from re-hashing an exchange that already occurred: Allan v Epp, 2018 ABQB 85 (CanLII) at para 65.
Repetitive and abusive questions have never been allowed: Rozak (Estate), 2011 ABQB 239 (CanLII) at para 31.
Such questions are “time-wasting, pointless and a violation of the Foundational Rules”: Allan at para 65; Milavsky at para 183.

[7] There are recognized exceptions when re-asking a question may be appropriate, and counsel does have a right to reframe or rephrase questions in order to obtain meaningful admissions: Allan at para 65
Braden v Knisley Estate, 2010 SKQB 335 (CanLII) at para 43.
Re-asking a question is acceptable when:
(1) the question has not actually been answered despite being asked
(2) new information is revealed that calls for re-visiting previous testimony, and
(3) counsel is simply reminding a witness of a topic previously discussed and confirming a previous answer: Milavsky at paras 180–182.

Information not Known to the Witness [8] In Wright v Schultz, [1992] 135 AR 58 (CA) at para 25, the Alberta Court of Appeal determined that an individual examined for discovery must only inform themselves on matters within the knowledge of anyone under their control, including employees and agents.
There is no obligation to attest to information outside their knowledge, or to inform themselves on matters outside their control: BN v Canada (AG), 1998 ABQB 786 (CanLII) at para 12.

[9] This Court confirmed that a witness's requirement to inform themselves on cross-examination on an affidavit is the same as on cross-examination for discovery in Canadian Western Bank v Alberta, 2003 ABQB 254 (CanLII) at para 18.
[10] One way to attempt to elicit information that is outside the knowledge of a witness is by posing hypothetical questions.

While hypothetical questions are not improper in themselves, they cannot become speculative, unrealistic or lack an air of reality: Maple Trade Finance Inc v Euler Hermes Canada, 2015 NSSC 37 (CanLII) at para 47
Dow Chemical Canada ULC v Nova Chemical Corporation, 2014 ABCA 244 (CanLII) at para 21.
In asking hypothetical questions, counsel must not
(i) go beyond the pleadings (here, Originating Application) to find a claim or defence that has not been raised
(ii) ask the witness a patently overbroad or vague question; or
(iii) ask the witness to comment on the actions or failures of other persons: Maple Trade at para 47.
Irrelevant Information [11] Rule 3.13 of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010 governs who counsel may question on an affidavit for an Originating Application.

In his commentary on this rule, Judge Fradsham notes that the examination under this rule may be “as searching and thorough” as examination on discovery; however, it must not “extend to matters wholly immaterial and irrelevant to the affidavit”: Judge Allan A Fradsham, Alberta Rules of Court Annotated 2019 (Toronto: Thomson Reuters, 2018) at 119).
[12] The Alberta Court of Appeal in Dow Chemical at paragraph 17 indicated that “relevance is primarily determined by the pleadings”.
When a matter proceeds by Originating Application, there is no opportunity for the respondent to file a document equivalent to a Statement of Defence.
However, that respondent, in this case Ms.

Moser, is still entitled to raise anything relevant and material to the claim advanced in the Originating Application, potentially capturing the “whole lawsuit”: Gill v 735458 Alberta Inc, 2003 ABQB 501 (CanLII) at paras 16, 35
Alberta (AG) v Alberta Power
(2000) Ltd, 2017 ABQB 195 (CanLII) at para 26.

[13] Thus, when questioning on an affidavit in support of an application, questions relevant to the underlying application are permitted, and if they are refused, the Court may order that they be answered: Rozak at para 30.
But issues relevant to the application are not confined to the “four corners of the affidavit”: Dow Chemical Canada ULC v Shell Chemicals Canada Ltd, 2008 ABQB 671 (CanLII) at para 7.

Cross examination may be “searching, thorough and not bound strictly to the material set out in … the Affidavit, but is limited to issues arising from the Affidavit as they relate to the motion”: Bond Street Properties Inc v Alberta Permit Pro, 2010 ABQB 416 (CanLII) at para 45 citing Colortech Painting and Decorating Ltd v Toh, 2000 ABQB 814 (CanLII) at para 26.

[14] In order to determine what information or documents are relevant in this matter, this Court must review the issues in the underlying Originating Application: Rozak at para 32. … Solicitor-Client Privilege [19] Solicitor-client privilege attaches to confidential communications between a lawyer and their client for the purpose of seeking legal advice: Descôteaux v Mierzwinski, 1982 CanLII 22 (SCC), [1982] 1 SCR 860 at 872-3
AARC Society v Sparks, 2018 ABCA 177 (CanLII) at para 2.
[20] This privilege extends to in-house counsel acting in their capacity as lawyers by giving advice or seeking instructions: NEP Canada v MEC OP LLC, 2013 ABQB 540 (CanLII) at para 25.
Whether the privilege attaches to a communication with in-house counsel depends on:
(a) the nature of the relationship
(b) the subject matter of the advice, and
(c) the circumstances in which the advice is sought and rendered: R v Campbell, 1999 CanLII 676 (SCC), [1999] 1 SCR 565 at para 50.
[21] This privilege receives significant protection during the discovery process.

Where a party asserts privilege over a document, the “obligation to provide sufficient information to indicate how a record fits within the claimed privilege does not require a degree of particularity that would defeat the privilege”: Canadian Natural Resources Ltd v ShawCor Ltd, 2014 ABCA 289 (CanLII) at para 56.

Solicitor-Client Privilege and Directors [22] When a corporation obtains legal advice, control over the privilege rests with its officers and directors: Adam M Dodek, Solicitor-Client Privilege (Markham: LexisNexis, 2014) at 410.

Thus, a Board of Directors as an entity enjoys “the right of unfettered access to legal advice provided to the corporation”: ibid at 411 [23] However, this right is truncated when a Director is in an adversarial position to a corporation.

In support of this proposition, the parties pointed this Court to two American authorities: Kalisman v Friedman, 2013 Del Ch LEXIS 100, 2013 WL 1668205; Chambers v Gold Medal Bakery Inc, 464 Mass 383 (Mass SC), 983 NE (2d) 683.
This statement of the law has also received support in Canadian authorities.

For example, in Livent Inc, Re, [1999] OJ No 5981 at para 4, 1999 CarswellOnt 4383 aff'd 2000 CarswellOnt 1890 (CA): I am of the view that, in a situation where a corporation is engaged in litigation with one or more of its directors, the right of those directors to access corporate records provided by the OBCA must be subject to any solicitor client privilege or litigation privilege of that corporation with respect to matters at issue in the litigation in the same manner as the right provided to a party by the Rules of Civil Procedure to disclosure of all documents having a semblance of relevance to the litigation is subject to such privileges.

To hold otherwise would lead to the ludicrous result that the director engaged in litigation with the corporation would not be entitled to access in his capacity as a litigant, but would be entitled to access in his capacity as a director, thereby indirectly negating the solicitor client privilege or litigation privilege of the corporation.

[emphasis added] [24] Similarly, in Wang v British Columbia Medical Association, 2011 BCSC 1658 (CanLII) at para 71, the Court found that documents were protected by privilege from the plaintiff after she was clearly in conflict with the Association because she had been cited for a breach of the code of conduct and had retained counsel.

paragraphs.text: (1) Oral questioning under this Part must be recorded word for word by a person qualified to do so (a) by a method that is capable of producing a written transcript, and (b) in a manner agreed on by the parties or directed by the Court. (2) The questioning party must make necessary arrangements to record the questioning. (3) Exhibits produced at the questioning must, unless otherwise agreed by the parties or ordered by the Court, (a) be incorporated in or attached to the transcript, or (b) be produced at the trial of the action without a notice to produce. (4) The person recording the oral questioning must (a) keep in safe custody the recorded questioning, (b) if required to do so, honestly and accurately transcribe the recorded questioning and deliver a copy of the transcript, as required, and (c) on or attached to any transcript (i) state the person's name, (ii) specify the date and place where the questioning occurred, and (iii) certify the transcript, or the portion of the questioning transcribed, as complete and accurate. (5) A person is qualified to record and transcribe oral questioning under this Part if the person is (a) an official court reporter, (b) a person appointed by the Court as an examiner under the Alberta Rules of Court (Alta. Reg. 390/68), or (c) a shorthand writer, sworn to record the questioning word for word and to impartially fulfill the duties imposed by subrule (4), who (i) is an agent or employee of an official court reporter or an examiner, or (ii) has been approved by the parties.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.27:1 Rule 5.27 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.27. 1. Overview In Signalta Resources Limited v. Canadian Natural Resources Limited, 2021 ABQB 867, 2021 CarswellAlta 2958, Justice Sidnell gave an overview of the operation of Rule 5.27, and a practical demonstration of the possible consequence (the exclusion of amendments made to answers given to undertakings) when the party providing the amended answers to undertakings does not comply with the Rule. [20] At trial, evidence can be entered by different methods and Rule 5.29(1) permits evidence given by a corporate witness to be read-in where the corporate representative, under oath, acknowledges the evidence as the evidence of the corporation. In this application, Mr. Kratz was the corporate representative, the person providing evidence and he acknowledged under oath that it was the evidence of the corporation. Under Rule 5.4(3), Mr. Kratz's evidence is the evidence of CNRL. Rule 5.30(1) provides for undertakings to be given during questioning and these undertakings are part of the questioning which is given under oath. Responses to undertakings can be the subject of cross-examination and a transcript can be produced. Allowing read-ins from testimony or responses to undertakings at trial contributes to trial efficiency and at the same time maintains the reliable evidence safeguard by requiring such evidence to be given under oath. [21] The corporate representative has an obligation under Rule 5.4(2) to be reasonably prepared to answer questions on behalf of the corporation. Mr. Kratz answered questions on the record and 294 undertakings, all of which were given under oath. [22] However, even the most honest and hardworking corporate representatives can make errors or come across information that brings into question an earlier answer to a question or undertaking. In that case, under Rule 5.27(1), the corporate representative must correct the initial answer if that answer was incorrect or misleading, or becomes incorrect or misleading as a result of new information. This correction must be made by affidavit which is served on each of the other parties as soon as practicable after the person realizes that the answer was, or has become, incorrect or misleading. Requiring affidavit evidence maintains the safeguard of evidence being given under oath. Requiring the affidavit to be produced as soon as practicable avoids ambush at trial. Upon receipt of the affidavit correcting the earlier evidence, the opposing party has the opportunity to cross-examine the corporate representative to delve into the reasons why the evidence changed, who was involved in identifying the changes to the evidence, how it changed and when the corporation knew it changed. Depending on the case, these may be critical lines of enquiry. [23] If Rule 5.27 is not complied with, and there is no affidavit setting out the corrections to the earlier evidence, the opposing party loses the opportunity to cross-examine the corporate representative on the changes to the evidence and may be prejudiced. Parties are entitled to rely on evidence from questioning in preparation for trial and to read-in that evidence at trial. [24] In this case, the parties have been ready to proceed to trial for more than two years. Five days before trial was set to begin, CNRL issued corrections to the evidence which SRL relied on, and, if those corrections are permitted, SRL will lose its evidence without knowing the reasons for the changes. While this situation may not be indicative of purposeful ambush at trial, the result is clearly prejudicial to SRL. I find that it does not matter whether the evidence SRL seeks to rely on evaporates on the eve of trial as a result of a corporate officer being highly diligently, as CNRL asserts that Mr. Harvey is being, or as a result of nefarious or obstructionist actions taken by an opposing party. In either scenario, the party receiving corrected evidence, without an affidavit pursuant to Rule 5.27(1), is prejudiced by not having the opportunity to cross-examine the affiant on the changes to the evidence and by being put in the position of not having the evidence that it planned to rely on at trial. In certain cases, last-minute changes to evidence, even if corrected by an affidavit pursuant to Rule 5.27(1), could entirely derail a trial. [25] CNRL asserts that Rule 5.27(1) states that a “person” must file an affidavit under Rule 5.27(1) and that since a “person” can be a corporation, and the corporate representative is giving evidence on behalf of a corporation, that the corporation can provide the required affidavit. There is no definition of “person” in the Rules. The definition of “corporate representative” is “a person appointed as the representative of a corporation under rule 5.4”. Clearly, the reference to “person” in Rule 5.27(1) means an individual as a corporation cannot be the corporate representative of a corporation under Rule 5.4. As a result, the “person” referred to in Rule 5.27(1) means the person who gave the evidence under oath in the first place, in this case, Mr. Kratz. If Mr. Kratz is no longer available to make a correcting affidavit, then that would have to be addressed, but that was not asserted in this case. [26] Regardless of how Rule 5.27(1) is to be interpreted, there was no affidavit setting out the corrections to CNRL's evidence. As a result of CNRL failing to follow the Rule 5.27(1), SRL had no opportunity to cross-examine on the corrections to the evidence that it relied on. The prejudice created by CNRL's non-compliance with Rule 5.27(1) can only be overcome by disallowing the amended responses to undertakings. As a result, SRL is permitted to read-in the original responses to undertakings and rely on them as part of its evidence in this trial, without any reference to the amendments. In McDonald v. Sproule Management GP Limited, 2023 ABKB 587, 2023 CarswellAlta 2651, Justice Marion said: [37] Rule 5.31 provides that, in certain circumstances, a party may use (or read-in) the evidence of the other party in a transcript of questioning under rules 5.17 or 5.18. Part 5 of the Rules does not specifically address whether undertaking answers form part of the transcript of questioning. There is an issue whether undertaking answers must be questioned upon under rule 5.30(2) (and presumably marked as an exhibit to the questioning) in order for them to become part of the Part 5 questioning transcript. In Signalta Resources Limited v Canadian Natural Resources Limited, 2021 ABQB 867, at para 20, Justice Sidnell noted that undertakings “are part of the questioning which is given under oath” and that “allowing read-ins from testimony or responses to undertakings at trial contributes to trial efficiency and at the same time maintains the reliable evidence safeguard by requiring such evidence to be given under oath”. [38] I agree with Justice Sidnell that undertaking requests are part of the questioning. In my view, the answers are also part of the questioning which are responded to later but nonetheless still subject to the oath. While rule 5.30(2) provides a mechanism to allow questioning on the undertaking answers (which could allow them to be marked as an exhibit), in my view it is not necessary to do that in order to have the undertaking answers form part of the transcript so they may be read-in at trial. Undertaking answers are part of the transcript of questioning under Part 5 of the Rules whether or not they are questioned upon because they form the belated answers to the questions that the witness was not able to answer at the time. In my view, while rule 5.30(2) is an important mechanism to explore, test, challenge or clarify the undertaking answers, it would be inefficient and impractical to require the questioning party to have the witness reattend for questioning in every case so that the answers could be marked as an exhibit.

Parties are entitled to rely on evidence from questioning in preparation for trial and to read-in that evidence at trial.
[24] In this case, the parties have been ready to proceed to trial for more than two years.

Five days before trial was set to begin, CNRL issued corrections to the evidence which SRL relied on, and, if those corrections are permitted, SRL will lose its evidence without knowing the reasons for the changes.
While this situation may not be indicative of purposeful ambush at trial, the result is clearly prejudicial to SRL.
I find that it does not matter whether the evidence SRL seeks to rely on evaporates on the eve of trial as a result of a corporate officer being highly diligently, as CNRL asserts that Mr.
Harvey is being, or as a result of nefarious or obstructionist actions taken by an opposing party.

In either scenario, the party receiving corrected evidence, without an affidavit pursuant to Rule 5.27(1), is prejudiced by not having the opportunity to cross-examine the affiant on the changes to the evidence and by being put in the position of not having the evidence that it planned to rely on at trial.
In certain cases, last-minute changes to evidence, even if corrected by an affidavit pursuant to Rule 5.27(1), could entirely derail a trial.

[25] CNRL asserts that Rule 5.27(1) states that a “person” must file an affidavit under Rule 5.27(1) and that since a “person” can be a corporation, and the corporate representative is giving evidence on behalf of a corporation, that the corporation can provide the required affidavit.
There is no definition of “person” in the Rules.
The definition of “corporate representative” is “a person appointed as the representative of a corporation under rule 5.4”.
Clearly, the reference to “person” in Rule 5.27(1) means an individual as a corporation cannot be the corporate representative of a corporation under Rule 5.4.
As a result, the “person” referred to in Rule 5.27(1) means the person who gave the evidence under oath in the first place, in this case, Mr.
Kratz.
If Mr.
Kratz is no longer available to make a correcting affidavit, then that would have to be addressed, but that was not asserted in this case.
[26] Regardless of how Rule 5.27(1) is to be interpreted, there was no affidavit setting out the corrections to CNRL's evidence.
As a result of CNRL failing to follow the Rule 5.27(1), SRL had no opportunity to cross-examine on the corrections to the evidence that it relied on.
The prejudice created by CNRL's non-compliance with Rule 5.27(1) can only be overcome by disallowing the amended responses to undertakings.
As a result, SRL is permitted to read-in the original responses to undertakings and rely on them as part of its evidence in this trial, without any reference to the amendments.
In McDonald v.

Sproule Management GP Limited, 2023 ABKB 587, 2023 CarswellAlta 2651, Justice Marion said: [37] Rule 5.31 provides that, in certain circumstances, a party may use (or read-in) the evidence of the other party in a transcript of questioning under rules 5.17 or 5.18.
Part 5 of the Rules does not specifically address whether undertaking answers form part of the transcript of questioning.

There is an issue whether undertaking answers must be questioned upon under rule 5.30(2) (and presumably marked as an exhibit to the questioning) in order for them to become part of the Part 5 questioning transcript.

In Signalta Resources Limited v Canadian Natural Resources Limited, 2021 ABQB 867, at para 20, Justice Sidnell noted that undertakings “are part of the questioning which is given under oath” and that “allowing read-ins from testimony or responses to undertakings at trial contributes to trial efficiency and at the same time maintains the reliable evidence safeguard by requiring such evidence to be given under oath”.
[38] I agree with Justice Sidnell that undertaking requests are part of the questioning.
In my view, the answers are also part of the questioning which are responded to later but nonetheless still subject to the oath.

While rule 5.30(2) provides a mechanism to allow questioning on the undertaking answers (which could allow them to be marked as an exhibit), in my view it is not necessary to do that in order to have the undertaking answers form part of the transcript so they may be read-in at trial.

Undertaking answers are part of the transcript of questioning under Part 5 of the Rules whether or not they are questioned upon because they form the belated answers to the questions that the witness was not able to answer at the time.

In my view, while rule 5.30(2) is an important mechanism to explore, test, challenge or clarify the undertaking answers, it would be inefficient and impractical to require the questioning party to have the witness reattend for questioning in every case so that the answers could be marked as an exhibit.

sentences.text: Written questions

paragraphs.text: (1) Unless the Court otherwise orders or the parties otherwise agree, the following rules apply with respect to written questions and the answers to them: (a) the written questions must be numbered and succinct; (b) the answers provided to the questions must be given by affidavit and must state the question being answered; (c) the party being questioned must serve the answers to the questions on each of the other parties within a time agreed on by the parties or ordered by the Court. (2) A party is entitled to ask (a) one set of follow-up written questions as a result of the answers to the initial written questions, or (b) follow-up oral questions if agreed by the parties. (3) If the answers to the written questions or the answers to the follow-up written or follow-up oral questions are unsatisfactory, the questioning party may apply to the Court for an order for either or both of the following: (a) oral or further oral questioning; (b) further written questions to be answered. paragraphs.text: 5.29. Acknowledgment of corporate witness's evidence
paragraphs.heading: Part 5. Disclosure Of Information

sentences.text: Acknowledgment of corporate witness's evidence

paragraphs.text: (1) The evidence given by a corporate witness during questioning may not be read in as evidence at trial unless a corporate representative of the corporation, under oath, acknowledges that the evidence forms some of the information of the corporation. (2) Subject to subrule (3), the corporate representative may refuse to acknowledge some or all of the evidence of the corporate witness and, if so, must state why, but is not entitled to refuse to acknowledge the corporate witness's information just because the corporate representative disbelieves or disagrees with it. (3) If the corporate representative disbelieves or disagrees with some or all of the evidence of a corporate witness, the corporate representative (a) must acknowledge the evidence as information of the corporation unless it is inadmissible under the laws of evidence, and (b) may then qualify the acknowledgment with further evidence that is contrary to or inconsistent with the corporate witness's evidence if the further evidence is based on either or both of the following: (i) the corporate representative's personal knowledge; (ii) a record prepared by the corporate representative or provided to the corporate representative by a person having personal knowledge of the issue in question.
